relations.note: Ipet and Taweret become effectively interchangeable in some later contexts while retaining distinct local theologies.
relations.source: Late Egyptian temple and funerary evidence

relations.note: Reret shares Taweret's hippopotamus form and protective functions, especially in astronomical and funerary systems.
Hedjet is a related protective hippopotamus goddess, though her precise identification with Taweret remains disputed.

relations.myth: Sobek issues as inundation from the Great One
relations.note: Sobek issues from the Great One, but identifying that maternal figure as Taweret is uncertain.
Taweret or Ipet is assimilated with Hathor through funerary settings and Hathoric crown iconography.
Protective Isis assumes hippopotamus-goddess forms, with explicit identifications in Ptolemaic temple and birth-house theology.

relations.myth: Joint protection of pregnancy or birth
relations.note: Mut and Taweret appear together on a Theban votive stela seeking maternal protection.

relations.myth: Joint protection of mother and child
relations.note: Bes and Taweret jointly protect domestic and birth settings; no ancient marriage narrative survives.
Plutarch calls Thueris Typhon's concubine, a late Greek relationship absent from earlier Egyptian narratives.
Thueris abandons Typhon's faction and transfers her allegiance to Horus.
Thueris joins Horus after abandoning Typhon, and Horus's followers destroy her pursuer.

relations.myth: Serpent pursues Thueris after her defection
relations.note: An unnamed serpent pursues Thueris until Horus's followers cut it apart.
Theban theology makes Ipet the maternal container in which Osiris is renewed.
Amun-Re emerges reborn through Ipet in the Opet temple's regeneration theology.

relations.myth: Divine regeneration within the maternal body
relations.note: Opet theology connects Ipet with Nut as the mother who receives and rebirths the solar god.
The celestial hippopotamus goddess restrains or guards the dangerous constellation identified as Seth's foreleg.
relations.source: Book of Day and Book of Night

relations.myth: Hippopotamus mother births the solar child
relations.note: Late texts assign a hippopotamus mother a solar-birth role, though her precise divine identity varies.

relations.myth: Returning Eye becomes a hippopotamus goddess
relations.note: Late temple imagery combines Taweret-like, lioness, Hathoric, Isiac, and inundation forms without establishing one stable narrative.

relations.myth: Taweret imagery becomes the Minoan genius
relations.note: Cretan artists adapted Taweret's visual form into a locally transformed ritual being.
